holidays.name: National Date Nut Bread Day
holidays.description: This is a day for slicing into a moist, sweet loaf. The loaf is studded with chewy dates and crunchy walnuts. Spread it with cream cheese or butter and have it with coffee or tea. It's an old-fashioned treat, and it fits well into the holiday baking season.
holidays.origin: It's an unofficial food observance, and nobody is sure who started it. It has become a regular part of the late-December baking calendar. Date nut bread itself became popular in early 20th-century American home kitchens.
holidays.funFact: Date nut bread was a favorite sandwich filler in the mid-1900s. People often spread it with cream cheese and served it as a tea sandwich.

holidays.name: National Cookie Exchange Day
holidays.description: Bakers get together and swap batches of homemade cookies. Everyone arrives with one kind of cookie and leaves with a varied assortment. You bake one recipe and end up with a whole holiday cookie platter.
holidays.origin: This is an unofficial observance of unclear origin. It grew out of the long tradition of holiday cookie swaps. Church groups and neighbors popularized those swaps in the United States.
holidays.funFact: A typical cookie swap works out simply. If 12 people each bring a dozen cookies, everyone goes home with 12 different kinds.

holidays.name: National Short Person Day
holidays.description: This is a lighthearted day for celebrating the vertically challenged. It's for everyone who has needed a step stool to reach the top shelf. It's a good excuse to laugh about the small frustrations and perks of being short.
holidays.origin: This is an unofficial observance of unclear origin. It falls on the shortest day of the year in the Northern Hemisphere, or very close to it. That timing makes the joke work.
holidays.funFact: The winter solstice usually falls on December 21 or 22. That is why the shortest day of the year pairs so neatly with a day for short people.
